claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 displays limited amorphous retention when rapidly quenched.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 has a complicated, low-stability thermal response upon reheating.
Adding a minor amount of Nb to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will improve amorphous retention.
Adding a minor amount of Nb will enhance the alloy's thermal stability upon reheating.
Nb can be introduced either by partially substituting for a transition metal or by adding an additional small fraction.
Nb is expected to increase atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Nb is expected to increase chemical disorder in the alloy.
The increased size mismatch and chemical disorder will frustrate nucleation of crystalline phases.
Nb will depress the critical nucleation temperature.
Nb-induced packing frustration will slow crystallization kinetics.
Slower crystallization kinetics will stabilize the amorphous phase during rapid quenching and subsequent thermal cycling.
The Nb-modified alloy will retain more amorphous material across a broader range of cooling rates than the baseline alloy.
The Nb-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature during reheating than the baseline alloy.
The beneficial effect is expected at moderately rapid cooling rates.
At extremely slow cooling rates, crystallization will dominate and Nb may not produce robust amorphous formation.
At sufficiently high cooling rates, both the baseline and Nb-modified alloys may remain amorphous, making the Nb benefit undetectable.
The benefit of Nb may disappear when its concentration lies outside an optimal composition window.
Nb content and cooling rate can affect the solidification structure of a related CoCrFeNiNbx alloy.
DSC, XRD, and microscopy can be used to compare reheating behavior, phase state, and microstructural homogeneity between baseline and Nb-modified samples.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant increase in amorphous retention and crystallization temperature under matched processing conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
